title: Gangtok food guide: momo, thukpa, gundruk and more
meta_description: What to eat in Gangtok: momo, thukpa, sel roti, gundruk, churpi, phagshapa, kinema and Temi tea, with the communities behind each dish and 2026 prices.
summary: Gangtok's food comes from three kitchens: Tibetan and Bhutia (momo, thukpa, phagshapa), Nepali (sel roti, gundruk, dal-bhat, sinki) and Lepcha and Limbu (kinema, tongba, millet and bamboo dishes). Eat momos and thukpa for under ₹250 a meal, look for gundruk and churpi in local thalis, and try phagshapa if you eat pork.

sections.heading: Three kitchens on one ridge
paras: Sikkim's food reflects who lives here. The Bhutia and Tibetan families brought noodle soups, dumplings and butter tea; the Nepali-speaking majority brought rice, lentils, fermented greens and the festival breads of Dasain and Tihar; the Lepcha and Limbu, among the oldest communities of the hills, have their own fermented foods, millet beers and forest vegetables. In Gangtok all three meet on the same menu, often in the same small kitchen behind MG Marg.

Fermentation is the thread that ties them together. The microbiologist Jyoti Prakash Tamang, who has spent decades studying the region's foods and wrote Himalayan Fermented Foods (CRC Press, 2010), describes dozens of fermented foods made in the Sikkim Himalaya, from leafy gundruk to soybean kinema and hard churpi cheese. They are a practical answer to long winters and steep fields, and they are why so many Sikkimese dishes taste sour, smoky or deep.

Sikkim also declared itself a fully organic farming state in 2016, which means its vegetables, ginger, turmeric and large cardamom come from farms that have phased out chemical fertilisers and pesticides. You will taste the difference most in simple things: a plate of saag, a bowl of dal.

sections.heading: Momo, thukpa and the Tibetan table
paras: The momo is Gangtok's everyday food. Small eateries steam them in stacked aluminium pots from morning to night, and a plate of eight to ten costs about ₹80–150 in 2026. Pork and chicken are the local favourites; vegetable, cheese and paneer versions are everywhere. Ask for the soup that comes with them, a clear broth, and the red chilli sauce, which in Sikkim is often made with dalle khursani, the round, fiery local chilli. Kothey momos are pan-fried on one side; fried momos are crisp all over.

Thukpa is a noodle soup with vegetables or meat, and thenthuk is its cousin with hand-pulled flat noodles. On a cold evening in December either is the best meal in town for under ₹200. Shaphaley, a fried bread pocket filled with minced meat, and gyathuk, another noodle soup, turn up on the menus of Tibetan-run places. Butter tea, salted and churned, is an acquired taste worth trying once.

A word on beef and pork, since guests ask. Pork is the everyday meat of Bhutia, Lepcha and many Nepali-speaking families, and beef is served in some Tibetan-run places but not in most Nepali Hindu homes, where it is avoided. Menus usually say clearly what is inside. Chicken and vegetable momos are on every menu, and cheese momos, made with local soft cheese, are a Gangtok favourite with children.

sections.heading: Phagshapa, churpi and Bhutia home food
paras: Phagshapa is the dish many Sikkimese name first when asked about home food: strips of pork fat cooked slowly with radish and dried red chillies, with no oil added because the fat renders its own. It is rich and fiery and best with plain rice. You find it more often in family kitchens and local restaurants than on tourist menus, so ask for it.

Churpi comes in two forms. Soft churpi, a fresh cottage cheese, is cooked into curries and pickles; the most famous is a fierce mix of churpi and dalle khursani. Hard churpi is made from yak or cow milk, dried until it is rock hard, and sold on strings in Lal Market. You chew a piece slowly for an hour, and hill families have long carried it on journeys. Buy a small packet; it keeps for months.

sections.heading: Sel roti, gundruk and the Nepali kitchen
paras: The daily meal for most families in Sikkim is dal-bhat-tarkari: rice, lentils, a vegetable dish and a pickle. Local thalis in Gangtok follow the same pattern for about ₹150–250, and the best ones add a small bowl of gundruk ko jhol, a sour soup of fermented greens. Gundruk is made by wilting mustard, radish or cauliflower leaves, packing them tight to ferment for a week or more and drying them in the sun. Sinki is the same idea applied to radish roots.

Sel roti is the festival bread of the Nepali-speaking communities: a rice-flour batter, sweetened and poured in a ring into hot oil. Families make it in large batches for Dasain and Tihar in October and November, but stalls sell it all year, especially in the mornings with tea. Kinema, fermented soybean with a strong smell and savoury taste, belongs to the Limbu and other Nepali-speaking communities and is cooked as a curry.

In winter, look out for families drying radish strips and greens on bamboo mats on rooftops and balconies around Gangtok; that is sinki and gundruk being made, the same way it has been done for generations.
list: Gundruk ko jhol: sour soup of fermented greens, best in winter
Sinki: fermented radish, in soups and pickles
Sel roti: ring-shaped rice bread, best warm in the morning
Kinema: fermented soybean curry, ask in local thali places
Dalle khursani achar: round chilli pickle, use with care

sections.heading: Tongba, chhaang and Temi tea
paras: Tongba is millet that has been fermented, packed into a wooden or bamboo vessel and topped up with hot water; you sip the warm, mild beer through a bamboo straw and add more water as you go. It belongs to the Limbu tradition and is shared at gatherings. Chhaang is the general name for fermented grain drinks across the Himalaya. Some local restaurants serve them; drink slowly, and not before a high-altitude day.

Sikkim's own tea comes from Temi Tea Garden in Namchi district, the state's tea estate, which sits on the slopes below Tendong Hill and was set up in 1969. It is sold in Gangtok's shops and makes a good small gift. Large cardamom, which Sikkim grows in the shade of alder trees, is the other thing to take home, along with dried churpi and dalle khursani pickle.

sections.heading: Where and how to eat well
paras: We do not name restaurants here because kitchens and cooks change, but the pattern is reliable. The small places in the lanes off MG Marg and around Lal Market serve office workers, students and drivers, turn their food over fast and charge fair prices. MG Marg's cafés charge city prices for coffee and cakes; enjoy one and eat lunch where the taxi drivers eat. For home food such as phagshapa and gundruk, a homestay on the Rumtek road or a village stay is the best kitchen of all.

A few practical notes. Vegetarians eat well everywhere, and Jain food can be arranged with notice at most mid-range hotels. Pork and beef are common on Tibetan and Bhutia menus; ask if you avoid either. Tap water should not be drunk unfiltered; carry a refillable bottle and fill it at your hotel. Sikkim restricts packaged water bottles in some areas at times, and the habit saves money. Most small eateries take UPI; carry some cash for stalls.

faqs.q: What is the most famous food of Gangtok?
faqs.a: The momo, steamed dumplings filled with pork, chicken, cheese or vegetables, served with a clear soup and a hot chilli sauce. A plate costs about ₹80–150 in a local eatery in 2026. Thukpa, a noodle soup, comes a close second. For something truly Sikkimese, try phagshapa, gundruk soup or a churpi and dalle khursani pickle.

Phagshapa is a Bhutia dish of pork fat strips stewed with radish and dried red chillies, cooked without added oil because the fat renders its own. It is rich, spicy and eaten with plain rice. It appears more in family kitchens and local restaurants than tourist menus, so ask for it, or try it at a homestay.

faqs.q: What is gundruk and how is it eaten?
faqs.a: Gundruk is a fermented, sun-dried leafy green made from mustard, radish or cauliflower leaves, a staple of the Nepali-speaking communities of Sikkim. It is cooked into a sour soup, gundruk ko jhol, or made into a pickle. Look for it in local thalis in Gangtok, especially in winter, when fresh greens are scarce.

Churpi is cheese from cow or yak milk. Soft churpi is a fresh cottage cheese cooked into curries and pickles, famously with the round dalle khursani chilli. Hard churpi is dried until rock hard and chewed slowly for an hour or more. You can buy hard churpi on strings at Lal Market; it keeps for months.

faqs.q: Is vegetarian food easy to find in Gangtok?
faqs.a: Yes. Vegetable momos, thukpa, dal-bhat thalis, paneer dishes and North and South Indian food are available everywhere, and most mid-range hotels can cook Jain meals with notice. Sikkim is a certified organic farming state, so simple vegetable dishes are often the best food on the menu. Ask whether soups use meat stock if you are strict.

Sel roti is a sweet, ring-shaped bread of rice-flour batter deep-fried in oil, made by the Nepali-speaking communities of Sikkim, especially for Dasain and Tihar in October and November. Stalls in Gangtok sell it through the year, best warm in the morning with tea, for about ₹20–40 a piece in 2026.

faqs.q: What local drinks should I try in Sikkim?
faqs.a: Tongba, the Limbu millet beer sipped warm through a bamboo straw, and chhaang, a fermented grain drink, are the traditional ones. Butter tea is the Tibetan staple. For tea, try Temi tea from Sikkim's own tea garden in Namchi district. Go easy on alcohol before a high-altitude day to Tsomgo or North Sikkim.

faqs.q: What food can I take home from Gangtok?
faqs.a: Temi tea, large cardamom, hard churpi, dalle khursani pickle and dried gundruk all travel well. Buy them at Lal Market or the shops around MG Marg. Pickles should be sealed for flights. Dalle khursani is among the hottest chillies in India, so warn whoever receives it.

faqs.q: Is street food safe in Gangtok?
faqs.a: Generally yes, if you eat where locals queue and food is cooked fresh in front of you. Steamed momos and hot soups are low risk. Avoid raw salads from unknown stalls and unfiltered water, and carry a refillable bottle filled with your hotel's filtered water. Ask before you eat dalle khursani pickle: it is very hot.
